note: The canonical standard for Hercules delivery documents, and the single source the linter, the authoring skill and the command templates are all written from — so what an author is told and what gets checked cannot drift apart. `rules` is the mechanical half: things that are true or false without an opinion. `guidance` is the judgement half, which is taught and never gated.

scenario_line.describes: One scenario per line: an identifier, a trigger, an arrow, and an observable outcome. A bullet that does not open with an identifier is ordinary prose, not a malformed scenario.

suggestion_closing_sentence: These are suggestions from Product, not decisions. Design owns the technical choice.

sections.name: Goal
sections.mandate: The problem in the user's words, and the change wanted.

sections.name: Users
sections.mandate: Each actor, and how they cope today without this.

sections.name: Scope
sections.mandate: In scope and out of scope, as noun phrases. Out of scope is never empty.

sections.name: Flows
sections.mandate: Per flow: a story line, then main, negative and corner scenario lines.

sections.name: Constraints
sections.mandate: Business, time, regulatory and integration constraints.

sections.name: Success criteria
sections.mandate: Measurable, each carrying a number or a named standard.

sections.name: Risks & unknowns
sections.mandate: Future risks and open assumptions. Mitigation plans belong in the spec.

sections.name: Technical suggestions (non-binding)
sections.mandate: The only place technical vocabulary is legal, and only as a suggestion.

sections.name: Design references
sections.mandate: Links to visual artifacts. Links only, never inline content.

sections.name: Challenge
sections.mandate: The one prose slot: the requirement restated, and the single hardest thing.

sections.name: Scope
sections.mandate: What this spec delivers, and the service it belongs to.

sections.name: Affected code
sections.mandate: Existing classes, methods and modules this touches. Each named, or marked NEW.

sections.name: Decision record
sections.mandate: Decision, chosen, rejected and why, risk, mitigation, revisit-when.

sections.name: Structure & patterns
sections.mandate: Each pattern named, with why, and one real use case. Deviations carry a why.

sections.name: Naming contract
sections.mandate: Domain vocabulary, names rejected, and why rejected.

sections.name: Implementation
sections.mandate: Key technical decisions and the constraints the code-of-conduct binds.

sections.name: Rules — DO / DON'T
sections.mandate: Two columns, imperative, each row independently testable.

sections.name: Risks & mitigations
sections.mandate: Risk, the signal that it is happening, the mitigation, and who owns it at build.

sections.name: Test suite
sections.mandate: Unit, integration, API and end-to-end scenarios, plus what must never be mocked.

sections.name: Acceptance criteria
sections.mandate: Given / When / Then per deliverable, each bound to a scenario identifier.

sections.name: Known violations
sections.mandate: Architecture or dependency rules expected to fail at scaffold time.

sections.name: Deletion note
sections.mandate: How this spec retires once its feature is delivered in code.

rules.title: required section missing
rules.fix: add the section, or say why this document does without it

rules.title: sections out of order
rules.fix: reorder to match `doc_lint.py template`, so readers find things where they expect

rules.title: placeholder text
rules.fix: write the real content, or delete the section — an empty section is omitted, never stubbed

rules.title: required section is empty
rules.fix: fill it, or delete it if nothing real belongs there

rules.title: unknown section heading
rules.fix: rename it to a section the standard defines, or move the content under one

rules.title: implementation detail outside the suggestions section
rules.fix: move it under the non-binding suggestions, or say it in business language

rules.title: technical mandate in a business document
rules.fix: state the outcome the business needs; the technical choice belongs to Design

rules.title: suggestion reads as a decision
rules.fix: hedge it, and close the section with its fixed sentence

rules.title: flow has no failure case
rules.fix: add a negative scenario, or mark the flow 'scenarios: n/a' with a reason

rules.title: malformed scenario line
rules.fix: write it as '- M1 | trigger -> observable outcome'

rules.title: fewer failure cases than happy paths
rules.fix: add negative scenarios — the failure space is unexamined, not absent

rules.title: duplicate scenario identifier
rules.fix: give each scenario its own identifier; identifiers are never reused

rules.title: more scenarios than the tier suggests
rules.fix: cut to the budget, or split the feature into two specs

rules.title: filename does not match the pattern
rules.fix: rename to the dated, kebab-case form the standard defines

rules.title: risk row carries no mitigation
rules.fix: state the mitigation, or record it in the requirements as an accepted risk

rules.title: shorter than this tier usually warrants
rules.fix: go deeper, or lower the tier if the depth is genuinely not needed

rules.title: longer than this tier usually warrants
rules.fix: cut, or move evidence and long enumerations into an appendix file

rules.title: reference does not resolve
rules.fix: point it at a section that exists, or correct the filename

rules.title: scenario identifier names nothing
rules.fix: point covers: at a scenario that exists in the requirements, or add the scenario

guidance.note: Judgement the checker deliberately does not make. The authoring skill and the command templates are written from this list, so a person learns these rather than being refused by them. Nothing here is scored, counted, or gated.

writing.do: Lead with the answer, then the reason in at most one sentence.
writing.dont: Open with context and arrive at the point three lines later.
writing.why: A reader scanning for a decision should find it in the first line of the section.

writing.topic: Words of degree carry a number
writing.do: Token validation stays under 200 ms at the gateway.
writing.why: Fast means a different thing to each reader, so it settles no argument.

writing.do: The claim MUST be taken before the row moves.
writing.dont: The claim is taken before the row moves.
writing.why: Bullets drop the subject and the modality a sentence carries, which is how a terse document ends up more ambiguous than a wordy one.

writing.do: Returns 200, 409 or 503, and no other status.
writing.why: An unfinished list is read as permission to invent the rest.

writing.do: Delete a section that has nothing real in it, heading included.
writing.dont: Leave the heading with 'None identified' under it.
writing.why: A stub reads as considered-and-cleared when nobody considered it.

naming.do: Name the role: a store, a gateway, a calendar.
naming.dont: Name the vendor in anything but the adapter that wraps it.
naming.why: If changing the library would force a rename, the design has taken a dependency it did not mean to. This is CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md's own rule, applied to the spec.
If someone with no context cannot guess roughly what it does, the name is carrying nothing and the reader has to go and look.

naming.topic: Weak words to avoid in a name
naming.do: Say what it does to what.
naming.dont: manager, helper, util, processor, handler, data, info, temp.
naming.why: They name a category, not a job, and they fit anything.

scenarios.topic: Which corner cases earn a line
scenarios.do: Admit one that is irreversible, sits on a boundary already named, involves two actors or retries, or has bitten before.
scenarios.why: A matrix nobody finishes reading protects nothing. Record the rest on one 'Considered and dropped' line so the thinking stays visible.

scenarios.do: refused, and the next 3 free slots are offered.
scenarios.why: A tester has to be able to tell whether it happened.

length.topic: Depth follows the tier, not the template
length.do: Go deep at any tier; spend the research effort where the blast radius is.
length.dont: Pad a low-tier document to look thorough, or truncate a critical one to look tidy.
length.why: The budgets in this file are a signal that something may be off, not a target to hit.

references.note: The one hard block. A spec pointing at a requirements section that does not exist is not a matter of taste: the link is broken and traceability is already lost.
references.scenario_note: A spec's covers: names the scenarios it delivers. Each must exist in the requirements it satisfies — an identifier that names nothing is a promise to build something undefined.

review.note: The judgement half, made accountable. A reviewer fills in one verdict per category — silence is never a pass, exactly as the A2A protocol already requires of a Pass status. The tool never forms the opinion; it checks the opinion was formed for every category, and turns the severities into one decision so 'needs work' stops being a feeling.

severity_meaning.blocker: the document cannot be built from as written; work stops
severity_meaning.major: a real gap that will cost rework if it ships unfixed
severity_meaning.minor: worth fixing, will not cause rework on its own
severity_meaning.pass: examined and sound — name what was checked

policy.note: How many unresolved majors a tier tolerates before the draft goes back. A blocker always sends it back. Rounds are bounded so a review cannot loop forever.

business-requirements.asks: Is the real problem stated, and would the beneficiary recognise it as theirs?
Are these the flows that matter, and is the failure space examined rather than assumed?
Do the stories and scenarios name concrete, observable outcomes a tester could check?
Does every success criterion carry a number or a named standard?
Is what we are NOT doing stated, and is it the honest boundary rather than a formality?
Are the risks the ones that would actually bite, with the unknowns admitted?
Has a technical decision been smuggled in as a requirement?

spec.asks: Does this answer the business requirement it claims to satisfy, in full?
Is any sentence readable two ways by two engineers?
Is each choice justified against a named alternative, with the risk it carries?
Are the patterns named, warranted, and are deviations explained rather than silent?
Would a swapped library force a rename? Would a cold reader guess what each name does?
Does every risk carry a mitigation that would actually work, with a signal to watch?
Can each acceptance criterion become a named, automatable test?
Can this be built as described, with what exists today?

probes.note: Falsification, not proof. A probe kills a plan that cannot work; it never certifies one that can, because that would mean knowing the result of executing a plan without executing it. Budgets are deliberately small: an assumption too expensive to check cheaply is itself a finding, recorded as UNPROVEN rather than chased.

verdicts.PASS: ran clean against an expectation stated before the run
verdicts.FAIL: contradicted the plan — the draft goes back, and this is the whole point
verdicts.UNPROVEN: not checkable here; carried to approval as a named risk with an owner

probes.never_fake_note: A probe may stand in for internal units that do not exist yet. Faking the thing it exists to check makes it green exactly where production fails.

classes.checks: the library exists and installs at the version named
the API has the shape the plan assumes
the external endpoint is real and answers
the mechanism exists on this runtime
the data supports the requirement — column, nullability, volume
the main and negative paths connect end to end, with real external dependencies and hand-written stand-ins for unwritten internals
